texts.title: The Bones in the Museum

texts.title: The Day Everything Changed
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: About sixty-six million years ago, dinosaurs ruled the Earth. There were gentle giants that ate plants, fast hunters, and small feathered animals that ran between the ferns. Nothing suggested that their world was about to change, and no animal could imagine what was coming from the sky. One day, a rock from space, about ten kilometres wide, crashed into our planet. The blow was so strong that it threw a huge cloud of dust and ash into the sky. For months, the sky stayed dark and very little sunlight reached the ground. Without light, many plants died, and the animals that ate them ran out of food. After that, the hunters that fed on those animals went hungry too. Scientists know all this because of a thin layer of rock that appears in many parts of the world. It contains a rare metal that is much more common in space rocks than on Earth. It is like a fingerprint left behind by that crash. Yet the story did not end completely. Some small dinosaurs survived and, over millions of years, they changed into the birds we see today. Whenever a sparrow lands on your windowsill, you are looking at a descendant of those giants, and the story of the dinosaurs is still flying around us.

texts.title: A Map of Stars
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: Thousands of years ago, people looked at the night sky and searched for shapes among the stars. They joined the dots with imaginary lines, as in a drawing game, and that is how constellations were born. Some look like a bear, a hunter or a crab. Today we know eighty-eight of them, and each one covers a part of the sky. These pictures were not only for telling stories. Sailors used them to know which way they were sailing when they could not see the coast. Farmers watched which constellations appeared in each season, so they knew when to plant their crops. Although the stars in a constellation look like neighbours, they are really very far apart. They only seem close because we see them from the Earth, just as two distant street lights look as if they were side by side.

texts.title: A Year on Every Planet
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: On Earth, a year lasts three hundred and sixty-five days, which is the time our planet takes to travel once around the Sun. But every planet has its own path and its own speed, so the length of a year changes a lot from one world to another. Mercury, the closest to the Sun, is very fast and finishes its trip in only eighty-eight days. If you lived there, you would celebrate more than four birthdays every Earth year. Venus takes about two hundred and twenty-five days, and Mars almost two Earth years. Jupiter, the giant, needs twelve years to go around, so a twelve-year-old on Earth would have only one birthday on Jupiter. The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its path and the slower it moves, because the pull of the Sun is weaker. Neptune, the last one, takes one hundred and sixty-five years. Since people discovered it, less than two hundred years ago, it has completed hardly one full trip. This teaches us something interesting: the calendar is not a universal truth. It is a measure that we invented by looking at our own sky, and a visitor from another planet would count the days in a very different way.

texts.title: The Last Lap
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: Nora had been training for months for the fifteen hundred metre race. Every afternoon after school she put on her trainers and ran around the park. At first she got tired very quickly and her legs hurt, but little by little she noticed that she could run for longer without stopping. Her coach always said the same thing: "Do not race against the others. Race against yesterday's Nora." On the day of the race, the stadium was full. The starting gun sounded and all the runners set off together. Nora decided to save her energy during the first laps, exactly as they had planned. She was in seventh place and, although she wanted to overtake, she stayed calm and breathed steadily. On the second to last lap she began to catch up with the leaders. Her heart was beating fast, but she also felt a new strength. On the final straight she gritted her teeth and sprinted with everything she had left. She passed two runners, and then another. She crossed the line in fourth place, without a medal. But when she looked at the giant clock, she saw that she had improved her personal best by almost ten seconds. Her coach hugged her and said, "Today you beat yesterday's Nora." Nora smiled, because those words were worth more than any medal.

texts.title: How Animals Sleep
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: All animals need to sleep, but each one does it in its own way. Bats sleep hanging upside down, holding on to a branch or to the roof of a cave, and they can spend up to twenty hours a day like that. Dolphins have a curious problem: if they fell fully asleep, they would stop breathing, because they must swim up to the surface to take in air. That is why they sleep with half of their brain at a time. While one half rests, the other half keeps watch and controls their breathing. Some migrating birds do something similar on long journeys, and a few even sleep for a few seconds while flying.

Each place on the planet has a slightly different magnetic strength and angle, so turtles may remember the magnetic fingerprint of their home beach. Near the coast, they also seem to recognise the smell of the water and the sound of the waves. Once on the sand, the female digs a nest with her back flippers, lays about a hundred white eggs and covers them carefully. Then she goes back to the sea without looking behind. Two months later, the babies hatch and run towards the water, following the shine of the moon on the waves. Sadly, city lights can confuse them and lead them the wrong way. That is why, on many beaches, the street lamps are switched off during the hatching season, so that the little turtles can find their way to the sea.

texts.title: Tricks of a Good Player
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: Daniel has been playing an adventure game for months, and he keeps getting better. It is not because he is luckier, but because he has found a few habits that help him. The first is reading the instructions and the messages on the screen carefully, because they often give very valuable clues. The second habit is learning from every defeat. When he loses, he does not switch off the console angrily. He asks himself what happened, what he could do differently and what to try next time. With that method, a level that seemed impossible is finally beaten. The third habit is resting. After an hour, Daniel takes a break to stretch, drink some water and look out of the window. That way his eyes and his head recover, and he plays more calmly when he returns. "A good player is not the one who plays the longest, but the one who learns the best," his aunt tells him.

It did not look like much, but it showed them whether moving around was fun. If something does not work in a prototype, it is much easier to fix it before drawing thousands of details. When they had the first level, they gave it to their friends to test. The players always got stuck in the same place, a jump that was too long. Alvaro made it shorter and, when they tried again, everyone passed it with a smile. They learned that designing a video game is like writing a story: you try, you correct and you try again. They also understood that working as a team makes the road shorter and more fun. Months later, they published the game for free. The best part was a message from a child who wrote: "Thank you, your robot made me laugh so much."

texts.title: Real Pirates
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: In stories, pirates hide treasure under the sand, but real life was quite different. Real pirates attacked ships to take their goods, such as cloth, spices or barrels of sugar. They rarely buried anything, because the usual thing was to share the loot among the whole crew. Life on board was not as exciting as the films make it look. They spent weeks far out at sea, eating food that was often hard bread and salted meat. To stay healthy they needed fruit with vitamins, and those who did not eat it suffered from an illness called scurvy. What is true is that pirates had a rather curious system of rules. On many ships, the crew voted to choose the captain, and any sailor could speak at the meetings. Someone who lost an arm or a leg in a battle also received some compensation. texts.title: What Is an Algorithm?
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: An algorithm is a list of steps in order that is used to solve a problem. It sounds complicated, but we all use algorithms every day without noticing. When you make a sandwich, you follow an algorithm: you take the bread, open it, put in the cheese, close it and that is it. If you change the order of the steps, the result can be very different. Robots work by following algorithms that somebody wrote beforehand. Imagine a robot that has to cross a room. First it checks whether there are any obstacles, and if there is a chair in its way, it turns right. Then it moves one step and looks again. It repeats the process until it reaches the door. The important thing is that the instructions are clear and exact. If you tell a robot to "walk a little", it will not know how much a little is. But if you say "move three steps forward", it will know exactly what to do. Programming means learning to explain things in so much detail that even a machine understands them.

texts.title: The Robot That Learned

The robot moved forward, left the line and ended up spinning in circles. Marina suggested a solution: if the left sensor saw white, the robot should turn a little to the right, and the other way round. It was a very simple rule, but it worked much better. Then Pablo noticed that on the sharpest bends the robot still failed, because it was going too fast. They added a new instruction: if both sensors changed at once, it had to slow down. On the tenth try, the robot finished the whole circuit without a single mistake. Their teachers explained that engineers work in exactly this way: they test, they observe what fails, they change a little and they test again. No machine is born perfect, not even the most famous ones in the world. What makes it good is the patience of the people who improve it, step by step.

texts.title: Where Dragons Come From
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: In almost every culture in the world there are stories about dragons, although each one imagines them differently. In Europe, dragons were winged, fire-breathing beasts that guarded treasure in dark caves. In China, on the other hand, the dragon was a kind animal, like a long snake without wings, which controlled the rain and the rivers and brought good luck. Scientists do not know for sure why there are dragons in so many places so far apart. One theory says that thousands of years ago, people found huge bones of dinosaurs or mammoths in the mountains and explained them as the remains of fabulous creatures. Another idea says that the fear of snakes, crocodiles and birds of prey, mixed together in a single monster, is shared by all humankind. The nice thing about dragons is that they have changed over time. Today they appear in novels and films as loyal friends, wise teachers or misunderstood creatures who only want to be listened to. They no longer stand only for danger, but also for what we do not understand at first. Perhaps that is why they still fascinate us. Everyone who draws a dragon adds something of their own: scales of a different colour, a different tail or a kinder look. So dragons live on thanks to the imagination of all of us.

texts.title: The Instruments of the Orchestra
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: An orchestra is a large group of musicians who play together. They sit in families of instruments. At the front are the strings, such as the violin and the cello, which sound when you rub or pluck the strings. Behind them are the wind instruments, such as the flute or the trumpet, which sound when you blow. At the back are the percussion instruments, such as the drum and the cymbals, which sound when you hit them. A conductor moves their arms so that everyone plays at the same time.

texts.title: Why a Guitar Sounds
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: When somebody plucks a guitar string, the string begins to vibrate very quickly from side to side. That vibration moves the air, and the moving air reaches our ears as sound. But a string on its own sounds very quiet. That is why the guitar has a hollow wooden body, which works like a loudspeaker and makes the sound bigger. The six strings of a guitar do not all sound the same. The thin ones make high sounds, and the thick ones make low sounds. Besides, the player can change the note by pressing a string with a finger against a small metal bar called a fret. That way, the part of the string that vibrates is shorter, and the sound is higher. With a little patience, anybody can learn. The hard part is not playing lots of notes, but playing a few notes well and on time. That is why musicians practise every day, even if it is only ten minutes, so that their fingers get used to it little by little.

questions.q: What does the wooden body do?
questions.ev: makes the sound bigger

questions.q: What sound do thin strings make?
questions.ev: The thin ones make high sounds

texts.title: The Music Box
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: In the attic of her grandmother's house, Carmen found a small wooden box with a golden dancer on the lid. When she opened it, a soft, slightly trembling tune began to play. Carmen recognised it at once: it was the lullaby that her grandmother used to sing to her when she was little. Curious, she looked at the mechanism. There was a cylinder with tiny metal pins, turning slowly. Each pin touched a steel tooth of a different length, and each tooth made a different note. The shorter teeth sounded high, and the longer ones low. Carmen understood that the whole tune was recorded in the position of the pins, like a message written in code. With a magnifying glass and a pencil, she copied the pattern on a sheet of paper. She drew a grid, with the notes going up and the time going across, and marked a dot for every pin. Then she asked her grandmother to show her how she played that lullaby on an old piano. She found out that her grandmother played it from memory, without any sheet music. That afternoon, grandmother and granddaughter played together, one with the music box and the other with the piano. Carmen thought that music is not only in instruments, but also in the love of the people who keep it and share it.

texts.title: Why Bread Rises
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: When we knead bread, we mix flour, water, salt and a pinch of yeast. Yeast looks like dust, but it is really made of tiny living things called fungi. These fungi feed on the sugar in the flour and, as they do, they give off a gas called carbon dioxide. That gas makes bubbles inside the dough. Because the dough is stretchy, the bubbles blow it up, just like when we blow up a balloon. That is why, after a few hours of rest, the dough doubles in size. When the bread goes into the oven, the heat makes the gas expand even more, and the bread rises a little further. In the end, the heat kills the fungi and the dough becomes firm, but the bubbles stay trapped inside. They are the holes we see when we cut a slice. The better the dough is kneaded, the smaller and more even the holes are, and the softer the bread is.

texts.title: Science in the Kitchen
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: Cooking is, deep down, experimenting with food. Every time we make a recipe, chemical and physical changes happen that we can see and smell. Understanding them helps us cook better and be more creative. A well-known example is the egg. When it is raw, the white is a clear liquid. As it heats up, the proteins inside it unfold and stick to each other, forming a net that traps the water. That is why the white turns solid and white. If you heat it too much, the net squeezes tightly and pushes the water out, and the egg becomes rubbery. Another case is the golden colour of toast or of a steak. When the surface reaches about one hundred and fifty degrees, the sugars and the proteins react with each other and create hundreds of new flavours and that tasty brown colour. This is called the Maillard reaction, and it happens with bread, meat and even roasted coffee. If you ever cook with the help of an adult, pay attention to these details: the change of colour, the smell rising from the heat, the texture that changes. The more attentive you are, the more you will learn, and the food will taste better too, because you will have made it understanding what is happening.

questions.ev: unfold and stick to each other

questions.q: What is the browning reaction called?
questions.ev: called the Maillard reaction

questions.q: What should you do when cooking with an adult?
questions.ev: pay attention to these details

texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)

Inside the tyre there is air under pressure, which is why it feels soft when it is not pumped up enough. Tyres also have small grooves that push the water away when it rains. If the grooves are too worn, the car can skid, so tyres must be checked often.

texts.title: How a Plane Flies
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: A plane weighs thousands of kilos and yet it stays in the air. It looks like a mystery, but the explanation is quite simple. The key is in the wings, which have a special shape: curved on top and flatter underneath. When the plane moves very fast, the air flowing over the wing travels faster than the air below it. That difference in the speed of the air creates a force that pushes the wing upwards, called lift. The faster the plane goes, the greater the force. That is why, before taking off, the plane speeds along the runway until it reaches the speed it needs. The engines, for their part, only push the plane forwards. To climb, descend or turn, the pilot moves some parts of the wings and the tail, and in this way changes the direction of the air. A glider, which has no engine, can fly for a long time using currents of warm air.

texts.title: From the Horse to the Electric Car
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: A little more than a hundred years ago, most people travelled on foot or by horse. The first cars were expensive, noisy and unreliable, and many people thought they would never replace carriages. However, within a few decades they changed cities completely, and the streets filled with engines. Petrol cars work by burning fuel inside the engine. That burning moves pistons, and the pistons turn the wheels. But it also produces gases that pollute the air and add to global warming. That is why many companies now build electric vehicles, which use a battery and a very quiet motor, and which do not send smoke out of an exhaust pipe. Not everything is perfect, because making batteries needs minerals that must be mined carefully, and the electricity that is used should come, as far as possible, from clean sources such as the sun or the wind. Engineers are working so that batteries last longer and can be recycled. Besides, more and more people choose shared transport: the train, the bus and the bicycle. Moving better does not only mean changing the engine, but also thinking about how much, how and why we travel. That is perhaps the great question of the future.

texts.title: The Tides
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: If you have ever spent a whole day at the beach, you may have noticed that the water goes up and down. This movement is called the tide, and it happens twice a day. At high tide, the sea covers a large part of the sand. At low tide, the water moves away and rocks, pools and shells appear that you could not see before. The main cause of tides is the Moon. Its gravity pulls the water of the oceans, and makes it rise on the side of the Earth that is closest to the Moon. The Sun also has an effect, but a smaller one, because it is much farther away. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in line, the tides are stronger. For fishermen and sailors, knowing the tides is essential. Some boats can only enter the harbour at high tide, and people who gather clams use low tide to work. And for children who look for crabs in the rock pools, low tide is the best moment of the adventure.

texts.title: A Forest Under the Sea
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: On the cold coasts of many countries grow enormous sea plants called giant kelp. They can be forty metres tall and grow half a metre in a single day. When thousands of them grow together, they form a real underwater forest, where the sunlight comes down in golden rays between the long leaves. These forests are not only beautiful, but also essential for marine life. They give shelter to thousands of species: small fish hide among the leaves, otters wrap themselves in them so the waves do not carry them away, and sea urchins feed on their stems. The kelp also absorbs carbon dioxide from the water, which helps to slow down climate change. However, these forests are in danger. Warmer oceans, pollution and the loss of the animals that keep the urchins in check have meant that, in some places, the urchins eat all the kelp and leave the seabed empty, like a desert. To bring them back, scientists plant young kelp on the seabed, carefully remove some urchins and protect the coastal areas. Some divers help as volunteers. Looking after the sea, even if we cannot see it from the shore, is also looking after life on the whole Earth.

texts.title: The Case of the Missing Biscuits
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: When Lucy came into the kitchen, the biscuit tin was empty. With her notebook under her arm, she decided to solve the mystery like a real detective. First she examined the scene: the tin was open on the table, and on the floor there were some crumbs that led to the garden door. Then she questioned the suspects. Her brother Peter said he had not left his room all morning, and her cousin Lola said she had been reading on the sofa. Lucy looked at them carefully. Peter had clean hands, but Lola had a little chocolate mark on her cheek. Even so, Lucy did not say anything yet. She followed the crumbs to the garden and found Rex, the dog, nibbling the last biscuit under the tree. Next to him was a chair that somebody had pulled over to reach the tin. Lucy understood that the dog had an accomplice. She turned to Lola and smiled: "Case closed. And next time, share the biscuits."

texts.title: The Library Mystery
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: The school library kept a secret. Every Monday morning, the librarian found a book out of its place, always from the same shelf: the one with the adventure novels. Nobody had seen who did it, and the door was locked every night. Marta, who was the sort of person who never leaves a puzzle unsolved, decided to investigate. First she made a list of suspects, and then she wrote down in a notebook what clues she had. She discovered that the moved book was always different, but its position was always the same: last in the row, sticking out a little. It looked like a signal. One evening, Marta stayed in the library until closing time, hidden behind a bookcase. At eight o'clock exactly she heard soft footsteps. It was the caretaker, an old man called Anselmo, who took out a book, looked through it lovingly and left it sticking out. When he saw her, he was not angry. He explained that since he was young he had dreamed of reading adventures, but he never managed to finish school. Marta told the librarian, and from that week Anselmo had a place of his own to read: a small armchair next to the window. The mystery was solved, and the library gained one more reader.

texts.text: In Sophie's neighbourhood there was no superhero with a cape, but there was somebody very special: Mrs Carmen, who sold bread. One day, Sophie found out the secret by chance. She saw an old man arrive, pick up a bag in silence and leave with a smile. Sophie wanted to know more, and the next day she asked the baker herself. "It is nothing unusual," she answered. "It is what anybody would do if they could." From then on, Sophie looked at her neighbourhood with new eyes. She understood that the real superpowers are kindness, generosity and perseverance. And she decided to help in her own way: she delivered the letters to the older neighbours and went with Mrs Carmen on Saturdays. Very soon, other children joined them.

texts.title: The School of the Brave
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: In a city of mountains and red roofs there was a school that was different from all the others. It did not teach maths or languages, but something much stranger: how to be a brave person. It was run by a silver-haired woman called Miss Aurora, who had spent her life looking after others. One day a new boy arrived, called Hugo, who was sure that he already knew everything he needed. He bragged that he was the strongest and fastest in his old school. Miss Aurora listened to him patiently, and then set him a challenge: to climb to the top of the bell tower without help, but without running. Hugo climbed slowly, step by step. On the way he found a bird's nest that had fallen, and without hesitating he put it back in its place. Higher up, an old lady who could not climb with her basket asked for his help, and he went with her half way. When he reached the top, he had taken much longer than expected. "You have failed the challenge," said Miss Aurora with a smile. "But you have passed what really matters." Hugo felt something inside him change. He understood that bravery is not about being first, but about stopping to help when someone needs it.
